sections.label: Overview
sections.purpose: Concise scholarly summary of the figure, name, tradition, and significance.
sections.body:
**Ratnasambhava** ​(*ratnasambhava*) — ‌Jewel-Born, South ‌· 'Born ​of ​the Jewel' ​— the ​Dhyānibuddha of ​the ‌southern jewel ​family — ​belongs to ‌the ​Buddhist tradition, ‌where it ​is catalogued ‌under ​the domain ​"Jewel-Born, South". ​The name ​means ​"'Born of ‌the Jewel' ​— the ‌Dhyānibuddha ​of the ‌southern jewel ​family"[^1].

**Ratnasambhava** ‌is ​the Dhyānibuddha ‌of the ​southern quarter, ​the ‌'Born of ‌the Jewel' ‌whose open ​palm ​bestows the ‌treasures of ​the Buddhist ​path. ‌Head of ​the ratna, ​jewel family, ‌he ​transmutes pride ‌and avarice ​into the ​wisdom ​of equality ​— the ‌insight that ‌all ​beings, like ‌all gems, ​share one ​nature.[^2]

‌PuniCodex records ‌the canonical ‌scholarly spelling ‌**Ratnasambhava** ​and serves ‌its temple ​at [its ​temple](https://punicodex.com/ratnasambhava/). ​The displayed ‌form is ​ASCII-equivalent — ​a ​description computed ‌from the ​displayed form ​itself. ​The plain ‌ASCII form ​*ratnasambhava* contains ‌the ​same letters: ‌no recovered ​diacritics or ‌special ‌encoding is ​claimed. The ​work here ​is ​consistent citation, ‌capitalization, provenance, ‌and cultural ​context[^3].

sections.label: The Name
sections.purpose: Etymology, transliteration, canonical spelling, name variations, and evidence preservation.
sections.body:
The ​name is ‌attested in ‌Devanagari as ​**रत्नसम्भव**. ​Etymologically it ​means "'Born ​of the ​Jewel' ‌— the ​Dhyānibuddha of ​the ‌southern jewel ​family"[^1].

The ‌canonical spelling ​**Ratnasambhava** ‌matches the ​conventional scholarly ​romanization. The ​plain ​ASCII form ​*ratnasambhava* contains ‌the same ​letters, ‌so no ​lost diacritics ‌or encoding ​transition ‌is claimed. ​The editorial ‌work is ​to ​fix one ‌reviewed reference ‌spelling, ‌preserve capitalization ​and provenance, ​and keep ‌the ​original evidence ​visible. The ‌displayed form ​is ​ASCII-equivalent — ‌a description ​computed from ‌the ​displayed form ​itself.

The ​letter-by-letter transformation ​runs:

sections.body:
The ​reconstructed ‌pronunciation of ‌the ​name ​is **/ratnasambhava/** ​— ​Restored ​scholarly ‌form.

Phoneme ​by ​phoneme:

- ‌**ratnasambhava** — ​The ‌canonical ​restored ‌form Ratnasambhava.

​For ​the ​modern speaker, ​the ​closest ‌approximation ​is: Read ‌"Ratnasambhava" ​using ‌the reconstructed ​pronunciation ‌above; ​the ‌conventional Latin ​spelling ​adds ‌no diacritic ‌marks.

‌The ​conventional ​spelling "Ratnasambhava" ‌is ​already ​written in ‌Latin ​letters; ​the ‌lowercase form ​"ratnasambhava" ‌differs ​only ​in capitalization.

​The ​pronunciation ‌given above ‌reconstructs ​the ‌sound ​world in ​which ‌Ratnasambhava ‌was invoked. ‌Modern ‌speakers ​should ‌not expect ​exact ​identity ​with ancient ‌phonology; ​the ​reconstruction ​is a ‌scholarly ​compass, ​not a ​performance ‌prescription. ​The ‌reconstructed pronunciation ​of ‌Ratnasambhava ​is explained ‌separately ‌from ​its ​conventional Latin ​spelling, ​which ‌adds no ‌diacritic ​marks.

sections.label: Mythology
sections.purpose: Core myths, primary narratives, and textual evidence.
sections.body:
The ​stories of ‌Ratnasambhava ‌place jewel-born, ​south ​at ​the center ​of ​a living ‌mythological ​world.

### Origins ​(Myth)

‌Ratnasambhava appears ​in ‌buddhist tradition ​as ‌jewel-born, ​south. The ​name's ​meaning, "'Born ​of ​the Jewel' ‌— ​the Dhyānibuddha ‌of ​the southern ‌jewel ​family", ‌shapes the ​narratives ‌told about ​this ​figure.

### Worship ‌and ‌Memory (Cult)

‌Devotees ​and later ​tradition-keepers ‌preserved ​Ratnasambhava in ​ritual, ‌text, and ​iconography, ​ensuring the ‌name ​survived into ‌the ​modern scholarly ​record.

​The ​myths of ‌Ratnasambhava ‌survive in ​fragments, ‌summaries, and ​later ​retellings. Each ‌version ‌reflects the ‌interests ‌of ​its tellers ‌— ​poets, priests, ​philosophers, ​and scholars. ‌The ​PuniCodex entry ​does ​not privilege ‌a ​single ​version; it ​gathers ‌the attestations ​so ‌that readers ​can ‌compare them. ​The ‌restoration Ratnasambhava ‌gives ​the ​figure a ​stable ​name around ‌which ‌these variants ​orbit.

sections.body:
No ​monument, ‌inscription, ‌or ​artifact in ​the ​current ​PuniCodex ​corpus ‌is ​yet ​assigned to ‌Ratnasambhava ​with ‌certainty. ​That ‌absence ​should ​be read ​honestly: ​for ​a ‌Buddhist ​name ‌of ​this ‌type the ​material ‌record ​is ‌expected ​to ​be ‌thin, and ‌the ‌primary ​evidence ​remains ‌the ​textual ​testimony gathered ‌in ​the ​Scholarly ‌Sources ​section.

‌Were ​such ​evidence to ​surface, ​it ‌would ‌take ​recognizable ‌forms: ​votive or ​dedicatory ‌inscriptions ‌naming ‌रत्नसम्भव, ‌sanctuary ​or ‌cult remains ​tied ​to ​jewel-born ‌and ​iconography ​matching ​its ‌traditional attributes ​(name ​and ​domain). ‌Each ​candidate ‌would ​be weighed ‌against ​the ‌reconstructed ‌form ​of ​the ​name before ​entering ‌the ‌scholarly ​record.

sections.label: Meditation & Reflection
sections.purpose: Contemplative or interpretive essay on the figure's enduring meaning.
sections.body: Ratnasambhava ​is the ‌Buddha ‌who ​asks what ​wealth ​is ​for. Born ​of ‌the ​jewel, he ​does ‌not ​hoard it: ‌his ​hand ‌is open, ​palm ​outward ​— the ​only ​mudrā ‌among the ​five ‌Dhyani ​Buddhas that ‌gives ​rather ‌than reassures, ​subdues, ‌meditates, ​or protects. ​His ‌teaching ‌is that ‌avarice ​is ​equality denied: ‌the ​delusion ​that my ‌gem ​and ​yours are ‌rival ​claims on ‌a ​finite ​world. To ​meditate ​on ‌the south-facing ‌Buddha ​is ‌to imagine ​a ​richness ‌that increases ‌precisely ‌by ‌being given ​away. ‌In ​an age ​built ​on ‌scarcity mechanics ​and ​attention ​economies, the ‌jewel-born ​one ​is quietly ​heretical: ‌he ​promises that ‌the ​wish-fulfilling ‌gem was ​never ‌a ‌commodity, and ​that ​the ​hand which ​opens ‌is ‌itself the ​treasure.[^1]
